# Meridian Airport Services — airside document set

This folder holds the airside operations handbook and the machine-readable
index of its sections. The handbook is the operative manual for anyone who
holds an airside badge. The index is maintained by the airside operations unit
alongside the handbook and is used by the unit's tooling to find a section by
its number, so the two are revised together.

Airside operations control: +44 20 7946 0812, staffed around the clock.
Permits and badge queries: the pass office, terminal 1, landside.

# Meridian Airport Services — airside operations handbook

Revision 11. Issued 6 April 2026. Held by every airside badge holder and by
every contractor working within the security-restricted area.

This handbook is the operative manual for the movement of people, vehicles and
equipment on the manoeuvring area, the apron and the landside service roads of
Meridian Airport. It is issued by the airside operations unit and approved by
the safety and compliance board. Where a site-specific variation in the
appendices differs from the body of this handbook, the variation applies to
the sites it names.

Airside operations control: +44 20 7946 0812, around the clock.
Duty airside operations manager: extension 4410 between 06:00 and 22:00.

## 1 Purpose and scope

### 1.1 What this handbook covers

Meridian Airport operates a single runway with a parallel taxiway system, two
passenger terminals, a cargo apron, a general aviation apron and a maintenance
base. The airside operations unit is responsible for the safe and orderly
conduct of activities on all of those surfaces. This handbook records the
standards that badge holders, vehicle operators, contractors and visitors must
follow while they hold an airside badge or an airside escort.

The handbook covers:

- access control and the issue, use and return of airside badges and vehicle
  permits;
- the conduct of vehicles on the manoeuvring area, the apron and the service
  roads, including speed limits, lighting and marking;
- radio and telephone communication with airside operations control;
- foreign object debris control and the reporting of surface damage;
- refuelling, fuel storage and the movement of dangerous goods;
- winter operations and the use of runways, taxiways and aprons in low
  visibility;
- occurrence reporting, investigation and the recording of safety actions;
- competence, training and the assessment of airside drivers;
- the management of contractors, visitors and plant equipment.

### 1.2 What this handbook does not cover

Air traffic control procedures, runway licensing, aircraft engineering and
airline ground handling agreements are held in separate manuals issued by the
units that own them. Where this handbook refers to a control instruction, the
instruction issued by air traffic control or by airside operations control
takes precedence over anything written here.

### 1.3 How the handbook is read

The handbook is read in the order the reader needs it, not from front to back.
Clause numbers are stable between revisions: a clause keeps its number even
when the text around it is rewritten, so a reference to clause 3.4 in a
training record still points at the same requirement. When a clause is
withdrawn, its number is retired and the fact is recorded in appendix E.

## 2 Definitions and abbreviations

For the purposes of this handbook the following terms have the meanings given.
Abbreviations are written in full on first use and abbreviated afterwards.

- **Airside** — the area beyond the landside boundary, comprising the
  manoeuvring area, the apron and the service roads inside the security fence.
- **Apron** — the paved area provided for the parking of aircraft, the
  boarding and disembarking of passengers and the servicing of aircraft,
  excluding the manoeuvring area.
- **Manoeuvring area** — the part of the aerodrome used for the take-off,
  landing and taxiing of aircraft, excluding the apron.
- **Airside badge** — the identity document issued by the airport pass office
  that entitles the holder to enter the airside area unescorted.
- **Airside escort** — a badge holder who holds the escort endorsement and who
  is responsible for visitors under their control.
- **Vehicle permit** — the document issued by airside operations that allows a
  vehicle to be driven inside the security fence.
- **Access gate** — a controlled opening in the security fence, listed in
  clause 4.3.
- **Service road** — the landside road inside the security fence that links
  the access gates to the depots, the cargo shed and the terminal forecourts.
  Service roads are not available to aircraft.
- **Airside driving permit** — the endorsement on a badge that allows the
  holder to drive an airside vehicle without supervision.
- **Manoeuvring area clearance** — the permission given by air traffic control
  for a vehicle to enter the runway strip or the parallel taxiway.
- **Foreign object debris (FOD)** — any object on a movement surface that has
  no operational purpose there, including dropped tools, packaging, stones and
  fragments of aircraft or vehicle material.
- **Marshaller** — a trained person authorised to direct the movement of
  aircraft or vehicles by hand signal.
- **Escorted visitor** — a person without an airside badge who is escorted at
  all times by an airside escort.
- **Landside** — everything outside the security fence, including the
  terminal forecourts, the car parks and the public roads serving them.
- **Low visibility procedure** — the procedure described in clause 9 that
  applies when the visibility or the cloud base falls below the trigger values
  in that clause.
- **Occurrence** — any event that has caused, or could have caused, damage to
  an aircraft, injury to a person, damage to airport property, or a hazard to
  the safe operation of the aerodrome.
- **Permit holder** — the badge holder to whom a vehicle permit is issued; the
  permit holder is accountable for the vehicle's compliance even when another
  driver is at the wheel.
- **Stand** — a designated parking position for an aircraft on the apron.
- **Vehicle marshalling area** — the marked area on the apron where vehicles
  wait when they are not required at the aircraft.

## 3 Governance, revision and enquiry

### 3.1 Owner

The airside operations unit owns this handbook. The unit is answerable to the
safety and compliance board for the accuracy of the standards recorded here
and for the training that carries them to badge holders.

### 3.2 Revision cycle

The handbook is reviewed twice a year, in March and in September. A revision
that changes a requirement is issued with a new revision number and a summary
of the change in appendix E; a revision that only corrects typography or
cross-references is issued without a number change. Badge holders are notified
through the airside operations bulletin, and the current revision number is
displayed at every access gate.

### 3.3 Enquiries and waivers

Questions about the interpretation of a clause go to airside operations
control, which answers them in writing where the answer is likely to be
reused. A waiver from a requirement in this handbook is granted only by the
duty airside operations manager, is time-limited, and is recorded in the
waiver register kept by the unit. No waiver may be granted for a requirement
that rests on the aerodrome licence.

## 4 Access control

### 4.1 The security fence

The airside area is enclosed by a security fence. The fence is inspected by
the security unit every day and any damage is reported at once to airside
operations control and to the security unit's duty officer. No person may pass
through, under or over the fence except at an access gate, and no gate may be
left open and unattended for any period.

### 4.2 Badge checks

Every person entering the airside area presents an airside badge at the gate.
The badge is worn on the upper body, above the waist, with the photograph and
the expiry date visible at all times while the holder is inside the fence.
A badge that is expired, damaged, or that does not match the holder is
refused entry and the pass office is informed the same day. Badges are not
lent, not altered and not photographed for any purpose.

### 4.3 Access gates

The gates below are the only openings in the security fence. Each gate has a
stated use and a stated class of user.

| Gate | Name | Location | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| G1 | North gate | Terminal 1 approach road | Badged staff and permitted vehicles |
| G2 | Cargo gate | Cargo apron road | Badged staff, cargo vehicles by permit |
| G4 | Maintenance gate | Maintenance base road | Maintenance staff and base vehicles |
| G7 | Service gate | Landside service road, west | Service vehicles, catering and cleaning |
| G9 | Emergency gate | Runway end, south | Emergency services only, opened by control |
| G11 | Depot gate | Northgate depot, east side | Depot staff and depot-based vehicles only |

G9 is kept locked and is opened by airside operations control on the request
of the emergency services. G11 opens onto the landside service road only and
gives no access to the apron or to the manoeuvring area.

### 4.4 Visitors and escorted access

A visitor without an airside badge is escorted at all times. The escort holds
the escort endorsement, briefs the visitor on the standards in this handbook
before entering, and remains within sight and hearing of the visitor for the
whole visit. The escort is responsible for the visitor's conduct and for any
equipment the visitor brings inside the fence. An escort may take no more
than four visitors at one time, and may not escort a visitor while driving.

### 4.5 Lost badges and permits

A lost or stolen badge or vehicle permit is reported to the pass office
immediately by telephone and confirmed in writing the same day. The pass
office cancels the document, issues a replacement and records the loss in the
access control system. A permit holder who cannot produce a permit at a gate
is refused entry until the pass office confirms the vehicle's entitlement.

## 5 Airside badges

### 5.1 Issue

Airside badges are issued by the pass office after the applicant's identity,
right to work and criminal record check have been confirmed, and after the
applicant has completed the induction training in clause 13. An application
for a badge carries a photograph taken at the pass office, not supplied by the
applicant.

### 5.2 Endorsements

Endorsements are printed on the badge and define what the holder may do:

- **D** — driving: the holder may drive an airside vehicle without
  supervision.
- **E** — escort: the holder may escort visitors without an airside badge.
- **M** — marshalling: the holder may marshal aircraft to a stand.
- **R** — radiotelephony: the holder may transmit on the airside operations
  frequency.
- **H** — heavy plant: the holder may operate plant above 7.5 tonnes.

Endorsements are granted after the assessment that clause 13.4 sets for each
one and are withdrawn by the pass office on the instruction of airside
operations when the holder fails an assessment or breaches this handbook.

### 5.3 Validity and renewal

An airside badge is valid for the period printed on it, which is not more than
five years from issue. The badge holder applies for renewal at least four
weeks before the printed expiry date. A badge that expires is surrendered at
the pass office and a new badge is issued after the checks in clause 5.1 are
repeated.

### 5.4 Surrender

A badge is surrendered at the pass office when the holder leaves the
employment of the issuing organisation, when an endorsement is withdrawn, and
when the badge is damaged beyond legible use. Organisations holding badges on
behalf of their staff keep a list of the badges they hold and confirm the list
to the pass office twice a year.

## 6 Vehicle permits and airside vehicle standards

### 6.1 Permits

Every vehicle driven inside the security fence holds a vehicle permit issued
by airside operations. The permit is displayed on the windscreen or, on a
vehicle without a windscreen, on a plate fixed to the vehicle's front face
where it can be read from outside. A permit is issued to a named permit holder
and to a named vehicle; it is not transferred to another vehicle without the
written agreement of airside operations. The permit holder is accountable for
the vehicle's compliance with this handbook.

**6.1.1 Standard validity.** A vehicle permit is valid for a period of 12
months and is renewed before the printed expiry date. The application for
renewal is made by the permit holder, carries the vehicle's registration, its
type and its normal place of standing, and is submitted to airside operations
at least two weeks before the permit lapses.

**6.1.2 Lapsed permits.** A vehicle whose permit has lapsed is not driven
inside the fence for any purpose, including a journey to the pass office to
renew it. Where a lapsed vehicle must be moved, airside operations arranges
the move and the vehicle is escorted for the whole journey.

**6.1.3 Withdrawal.** Airside operations withdraws a permit where the vehicle
fails a condition in clause 6.3, where the permit holder is found to have
lent the permit to another vehicle, or where the vehicle is involved in an
occurrence that the investigation shows the vehicle's condition contributed
to.

### 6.2 Applications and records

The application form records the vehicle registration, the make and model, the
maximum gross weight, the type of fuel, the normal place of standing and the
permit holder's name and badge number. Airside operations keeps the issued
permits, the applications and the withdrawals in the permit register. A
vehicle that is sold or taken out of service is removed from the register by
the permit holder within five working days.

### 6.3 Vehicle standards

Every airside vehicle meets the standards below before a permit is issued and
at all times while the permit is held:

- a service brake and a parking brake that hold the vehicle on the apron's
  maximum gradient;
- lights, indicators and a rotating or flashing amber beacon on the roof;
- a fixed or retractable yellow and black chequered marking on the front and
  rear faces;
- tyres without cuts exposing the cords and with at least 1.6 millimetres of
  tread over the central three quarters of the width;
- for a vehicle that tows, a tow bar and a breakaway cable or a second
  coupling;
- a fire extinguisher of at least 2 kilograms, serviced within the last year;
- a first aid kit and, for a vehicle that carries passengers, a spill kit.

A vehicle that fails a standard is taken out of airside service at once and
its permit is suspended until the fault is cleared and the vehicle is
presented again.

### 6.4 Marking and identification

Airside vehicles carry the permit holder's name or the organisation's name on
both sides in letters at least 50 millimetres high. Vehicles belonging to the
airport's own fleet carry the unit's two-letter code on the bonnet and on the
rear door. A vehicle that is not marked is treated as a visitor vehicle and is
escorted whenever it is on the apron.

### 6.5 Electric and hybrid vehicles

An electric or hybrid vehicle is charged only at a marked charging point.
Charging cables are routed so that they do not cross a taxiway, a stand
holding line or a fire lane, and the cable is removed before the vehicle
moves. A vehicle being charged does not block an emergency access route and
is not left charging while unattended on the apron for more than the charging
period recorded on the point.

## 7 Airside driving standards

### 7.1 Requirement to hold a driving endorsement

A person drives an airside vehicle only while holding the driving endorsement
on their badge. A person whose driving endorsement has been withdrawn may
travel as a passenger in a vehicle on airside business, and may drive a
landside vehicle on a public road, but does not drive inside the fence until
the endorsement is restored.

### 7.2 Give-way rules

The order of priority on the airport is:

1. aircraft on the manoeuvring area, whether moving or on stand;
2. emergency vehicles responding to an incident;
3. airside operations and security vehicles on patrol;
4. everything else, in the order of arrival at a junction.

An aircraft always has priority over a vehicle, and a vehicle never passes
between an aircraft and its marshaller. On the apron a vehicle gives way to
another vehicle that is towing; on a service road the give-way markings and
signs decide.

### 7.3 Speed limits

The limits below apply without exception inside the security fence. The sign
at the entrance to a zone states the limit for that zone; where signs are not
present the following applies:

| Zone | Limit |
|---|---|
| Manoeuvring area, within 50 metres of a live runway | 20 km/h |
| Manoeuvring area elsewhere | 30 km/h |
| Apron, within a stand safety area | 10 km/h |
| Apron elsewhere | 25 km/h |
| Cargo apron | 20 km/h |
| Service roads | 40 km/h |
| Depot yards and gate approaches | 15 km/h |
| Maintenance base roads | 25 km/h |

A driver reduces speed below the limit whenever a lower speed is needed for
the conditions, and always reduces below the limit when passing a stand where
an aircraft is being serviced. A driver who cannot read a zone sign states the
assumed limit in the journey log.

### 7.4 Use of beacons and lights

A vehicle on the apron or the manoeuvring area displays a flashing amber
beacon at all times, day, night and in clear weather. Headlights are used on
the manoeuvring area and the service roads whenever the vehicle is moving, and
dipped headlights only on the apron, to avoid dazzling a marshaller.

### 7.5 Parking, stands and marshalling areas

A vehicle is parked only in a marked parking area or a designated vehicle
marshalling area. A vehicle is not parked within 15 metres of a fuel hydrant,
within a stand safety area, on a painted walkway, or where it would obstruct
an emergency access route. On a stand, a vehicle is parked clear of the
aircraft's turning circle and clear of the equipment a handling agent has
placed there.

### 7.6 Distraction, alcohol and fatigue

A driver does not use a hand-held radio, telephone or any other device while
driving. A driver who must take a call stops in a safe place, applies the
parking brake and switches off the beacon before answering. A person who has
consumed alcohol or a drug that affects their driving does not drive airside
and reports the fact to their supervisor; the airside limit is the same as the
limit for driving on a public road.

## 8 Radio and communication

### 8.1 Frequencies and use

Airside operations control works two frequencies: the operations frequency,
used for the control of vehicles on the apron and the service roads, and the
manoeuvring frequency, used only with air traffic control and only by holders
of the radiotelephony endorsement. A vehicle that needs to cross the runway
strip calls air traffic control on the manoeuvring frequency; every other
vehicle call is made to airside operations control.

### 8.2 Call discipline

A caller states the calling unit, the message and "over", and keeps the
message short enough to be understood in one hearing. The phonetic alphabet is
used for registrations and callsigns. A caller who does not understand a
message asks for it to be repeated rather than guessing at it. A radio is not
used for social conversation and a personal name is not used as a callsign.

### 8.3 Radio failure

A driver whose radio fails stops in a safe place clear of a stand holding line
and reports the failure by telephone to airside operations control. A driver
who cannot report by telephone remains in the vehicle with the beacon on and
waits for a patrol. A vehicle with a failed radio completes no further apron
movement until the radio is replaced.

### 8.4 Mandatory read-backs

The messages below are read back in full by the receiving unit, in the order
they were given:

- a clearance to enter the runway strip or the parallel taxiway;
- an instruction to hold short of a runway;
- a change to a stand allocation;
- an instruction to stop a vehicle or a convoy;
- a low visibility procedure announcement or cancellation.

A read-back that is not acknowledged by the sender is repeated. If the
read-back is given twice without acknowledgement, both units treat the
frequency as unusable and move to the fallback described in clause 8.5.

### 8.5 Fallback

Where the operations frequency fails, airside operations control moves to the
fallback frequency printed on the reverse of every badge and announces the
move on the telephone tree. A vehicle that is moving when the failure happens
completes its journey to the nearest safe parking position and telephones the
control room for instructions.

## 9 FOD, surface condition and winter operations

### 9.1 Foreign object debris

Every badge holder picks up foreign object debris they see on a movement
surface, if it is safe to stop and pick it up, and reports it to airside
operations control if it is too large to move, if it is on a live runway, or
if it lies within a stand safety area. Debris that is picked up is placed in a
FOD bin and the find is recorded in the FOD log, which control reviews every
day and analyses every week.

### 9.2 Tools and equipment

A contractor who takes tools or equipment onto a movement surface accounts for
every item at the end of the task and confirms the count to airside
operations. An item that cannot be accounted for stops the task, is reported
to control, and is searched for before the surface is returned to use.

### 9.3 Surface damage

A driver who sees a crack, a rut, a raised edge or a hole on a movement
surface reports it to airside operations control with the nearest stand number
or taxiway designator. Control raises a works order and marks the defect until
the works team attends.

### 9.4 Winter operations

The winter plan runs from 1 November to 31 March. Airside operations control
decides when to treat a surface, and the works team treats the manoeuvring
area, then the aprons, then the service roads. A vehicle not required for
treatment stays clear of the manoeuvring area while treatment is in progress
and follows the convoy route published each morning.

### 9.5 Snow clearance priority

| Priority | Surface |
|---|---|
| 1 | Runway and parallel taxiway |
| 2 | Rapid exit taxiways and the main apron taxilane |
| 3 | Terminal stand rows A to D |
| 4 | Cargo apron and the general aviation apron |
| 5 | Service roads and depot yards |

### 9.6 Low visibility procedures

Low visibility procedures are triggered when the visibility falls below 600
metres or the cloud base falls below 200 feet. Control announces the trigger
on the operations frequency and records the time in the airside log. Under low
visibility procedures a vehicle not on essential business leaves the apron,
the speed limits in clause 7.3 are halved, and every vehicle movement is
reported to control from the stand holding line. The procedures are cancelled
by control when the visibility has stayed above 800 metres for ten minutes.

## 10 Fuel and dangerous goods

### 10.1 Refuelling

Refuelling is carried out by the fuel operator's staff with the aircraft's
operator in attendance. A vehicle is not started, and a stand equipment item
is not moved, within 15 metres of an aircraft that is being refuelled. A
vehicle that must pass a refuelling aircraft uses the route marked on the
stand plan and displays its beacon.

### 10.2 Fuel hydrants

Fuel hydrants are marked in yellow. A vehicle is not parked within 15 metres
of a hydrant pit, and a hydrant pit cover is not opened except by the fuel
operator. A hydrant that leaks is reported to the fuel operator and to airside
operations control at once and the area within 30 metres is kept clear of
vehicles.

### 10.3 Fuel bowsers

A fuel bowser is driven only by a holder of the driving and heavy plant
endorsements. A bowser is not parked under an aircraft wing, not left with the
engine running while unattended, and not driven through a crowded stand area
without a marshaller walking ahead. A bowser that is not in use is kept in the
fuel compound.

### 10.4 Dangerous goods

The movement of dangerous goods inside the fence is authorised in advance by
airside operations. The consignment note travels with the vehicle, the load is
secured against movement, and the vehicle takes the route agreed with control.
A spill is reported at once, the area is cordoned, and no attempt is made to
wash a spill into a surface water drain.

## 11 Personal protective equipment

### 11.1 Minimum equipment

Every person inside the security fence wears, as a minimum, high-visibility
outer clothing that meets the airport's published standard, and safety
footwear with a protective toe cap. The high-visibility garment is worn over
all other clothing, including waterproofs, and is kept fastened.

### 11.2 Additional equipment

The table below states the additional equipment required for the tasks listed.
The equipment is supplied by the employer, not by the airport.

| Task | Additional equipment |
|---|---|
| Working within 15 metres of a live aircraft | Hearing protection |
| Aircraft marshalling | Hearing protection and a high-visibility vest with the marshalling marking |
| Fuel handling | Fuel-resistant gloves and eye protection |
| Works on the manoeuvring area | Class 3 high-visibility clothing |
| Snow clearance on foot | Class 3 high-visibility clothing and a handheld radio |
| Wildlife control | Eye protection where a weapon or a pyrotechnic is used |
| Working at height on a stand | Fall arrest harness and a rescue plan |

### 11.3 Condition

Personal protective equipment is inspected before each use by the person who
wears it. A garment that is torn, a harness that has taken a fall, and a
helmet that has been struck are withdrawn from use and replaced. Equipment
withdrawn from use is not returned to the store as serviceable.

## 12 Occurrence reporting

### 12.1 Who reports

Every person who witnesses an occurrence reports it. The duty to report does
not depend on seniority, on whether the person was involved, or on whether the
occurrence caused damage. A report is made to airside operations control at
once by radio or telephone and is followed by a written report in the airport
reporting system before the end of the reporter's shift.

### 12.2 Categories

| Category | Definition | Report within | Investigation by |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Damage to an aircraft, or injury needing hospital treatment | Immediately | Safety and compliance board |
| B | Damage to airport property, or injury needing first aid | Immediately | Airside operations unit |
| C | A vehicle or person entering a runway strip without clearance | Immediately | Safety and compliance board |
| D | A near miss between a vehicle and an aircraft, or two vehicles | 2 hours | Airside operations unit |
| E | A FOD find above the size in clause 9.1, or surface damage | 2 hours | Works and airside operations |
| F | A failure of lighting, marking or signage on a movement surface | 4 hours | Works team |
| G | A breach of this handbook with no consequence | End of shift | Airside operations unit |

### 12.3 What a report contains

A written report states the time to the minute, the place by stand or taxiway
designator, the people and vehicles involved with their badges and
registrations, what happened, what was done at the time, and what the reporter
believes would prevent a repetition. Photographs are attached where the
reporter has them, and the originals are kept in the reporting system.

### 12.4 Protection of the reporter

A report made under this clause is not used to discipline the reporter for an
honest error. The airport treats the reporting of an occurrence as evidence of
a healthy safety culture, and the safety and compliance board reviews the
number of reports each quarter to check that reporting has not fallen away.

### 12.5 Investigation and actions

The investigating unit in the table above gathers evidence, interviews those
involved, and issues a report within 20 working days. Each finding is given an
owner and a date in the safety actions register. An action that is not closed
by its date is escalated to the board at its next meeting, and the register is
reviewed monthly by airside operations.

## 13 Competence and training

### 13.1 Induction

Every applicant for an airside badge completes induction training before the
badge is issued. Induction covers access control, apron hazards, FOD, radio
discipline, occurrence reporting and this handbook. Induction is delivered by
airside operations and is refreshed every three years.

### 13.2 Airside driving assessment

A driving endorsement is granted after a practical assessment on the apron. The
assessment covers the give-way rules in clause 7.2, the speed limits in clause
7.3, parking and marshalling areas, and the standard of observation the
assessor judges safe. An assessment that is failed may be retaken after seven
days, and a second failure is referred to the applicant's employer.

### 13.3 Radio assessment

A radiotelephony endorsement is granted after an assessment of call discipline
and read-back, both on the operations frequency and on the manoeuvring
frequency. The assessment includes a simulated radio failure and the fallback
in clause 8.5.

### 13.4 Additional endorsements

| Endorsement | Assessment | Refresh |
|---|---|---|
| M — marshalling | Hand signals under supervision | 2 years |
| R — radiotelephony | Simulated calls and read-backs | 2 years |
| H — heavy plant | Practical operation of the plant class | 3 years |
| E — escort | Escort duties and visitor briefings | 3 years |

### 13.5 Records

The pass office keeps the training record for every badge holder, including
the date of each assessment, the assessor's name and the result. A driving
endorsement lapses where the holder has not driven airside for 12 months; the
pass office restores it after a short reassessment with an assessor.

### 13.6 Visitors and contractors

A contractor's own competence scheme is accepted where airside operations has
approved it in writing. The approval records the tasks the scheme covers and
the documents the contractor must show at the gate. A contractor whose
approval has lapsed is escorted until the approval is renewed.

## 14 Contractors, visitors and plant

### 14.1 Contractor induction

A contractor working inside the fence completes the airport's contractor
induction before starting work, holds an airside badge for every person on
site, and names a supervisor who is present whenever the work is in progress.
The supervisor holds the escort endorsement where the work brings escorted
visitors inside the fence.

### 14.2 Permits to work

Work on a movement surface, work within 15 metres of a live aircraft, hot work
and work at height are carried out under a permit to work issued by airside
operations. The permit states the surface, the times, the equipment, the
isolation required and the person in charge. A permit is closed by the issuer
after the surface has been inspected and returned to use.

### 14.3 Plant and equipment

Plant is inspected before it is taken inside the fence and carries a
serviceable plant tag. Plant that is not tagged is refused entry. A plant item
that breaks down on a movement surface is reported to airside operations
control at once, marked, and recovered by the operator's own recovery vehicle
under escort.

### 14.4 Leaving site

A contractor leaves the site clean: tools counted, materials removed, spill
kits restocked, and any temporary marking lifted. The supervisor confirms the
state of the surface to airside operations before the permit is closed.

## 15 Wildlife and bird control

### 15.1 Scope

Wildlife control on the airport is carried out by the airside operations
wildlife unit. The unit records every sighting, every dispersal action and
every strike in the wildlife log, and analyses the log each month.

### 15.2 Reporting by badge holders

A badge holder who sees a bird flock, a fox, a rabbit, a deer or any other
animal on or near a movement surface reports it to airside operations control
with the location and the direction of movement. A sighting is reported even
when the animal is outside the fence, because the movement predicts where the
animal will cross next.

### 15.3 Dispersal

Dispersal is carried out only by the wildlife unit, which uses the least
force that will move the animal away from the movement surface. Pyrotechnics
are not used within 50 metres of a fuel farm or a hydrant, and are not fired
across a stand or towards the terminal.

### 15.4 Grass and habitat

Grass on the manoeuvring area is kept short enough to discourage roosting and
long enough to discourage flocking species. The works team cuts to the height
the wildlife unit sets and does not cut within the bird-breeding window of
April to July.

## 16 Emergency procedures

### 16.1 Alerts

An aircraft emergency is declared by air traffic control. Airside operations
control passes the alert to the emergency services, closes the roads the
emergency services need, holds all non-emergency vehicle movement, and records
the times of each action in the airside log.

### 16.2 Access for emergency services

The emergency services enter by the gate nearest the incident and, where the
incident is on the manoeuvring area, with the clearance of air traffic
control. Airside operations places a marshal at the gate to guide the first
appliance and to hold later vehicles until a route is agreed.

### 16.3 Rendezvous points

| Stand group | Rendezvous point |
|---|---|
| Stands 1 to 9 | Rendezvous point A, west of stand 5 |
| Stands 10 to 20 | Rendezvous point B, at the cargo gate |
| Stands 21 to 30 | Rendezvous point C, terminal 2 forecourt |
| Cargo apron | Rendezvous point D, cargo shed south door |
| General aviation | Rendezvous point E, maintenance gate apron |

### 16.4 Vehicle stand-down

A vehicle that is not an emergency vehicle stops clear of a stand holding line
when an alert is declared, switches off the engine unless the engine is needed
for the vehicle's function, and waits for control to release the movement.
Control releases movements one stand group at a time and records the release.

### 16.5 Exercise

The airport runs a full emergency exercise once a year and a review of the
response plan twice a year. Attendance at the exercise is recorded against
each unit, and the board receives the findings and the actions that follow.

## 17 Records and retention

### 17.1 Records held

Airside operations holds the records in the table below. A record is kept in
the system named, is retrievable by date, vehicle registration, badge number
or location, and is protected from alteration after it is filed.

| Record | Kept by | Retention |
|---|---|---|
| Vehicle permit register | Airside operations | 6 years after the permit ends |
| Badge issue and surrender record | Pass office | 6 years after the badge ends |
| Training and assessment record | Pass office | 6 years after the badge ends |
| Occurrence reports and investigations | Safety and compliance | 10 years |
| Safety actions register | Safety and compliance | 10 years |
| FOD log and analysis | Airside operations | 3 years |
| Wildlife log | Wildlife unit | 5 years |
| Airside log of control decisions | Airside operations | 5 years |
| Waiver register | Airside operations | 6 years after the waiver ends |
| Permit to work records | Airside operations | 3 years |
| Plant and equipment inspection tags | Works team | 3 years |
| Winter treatment records | Works team | 5 years |

### 17.2 Access to records

A badge holder may ask to see the records that concern them, and the request
is answered within 20 working days. An investigating unit may see any record
that bears on an investigation, and the board may see any record it needs for
its assurance work. Records are released outside the airport only with the
agreement of the unit that owns them.

# Appendices

## Appendix A — Glossary of airside terms

- **Apron road** — the marked vehicle route that runs along the front of a
  stand row and links the stand parking areas to the service road network.
- **Backtrack** — the movement of an aircraft or a vehicle along a runway or
  taxiway in the direction opposite to the one in use.
- **Blast fence** — the structure that deflects jet blast away from a walkway
  or a road.
- **Clearance limit** — the point to which a movement is cleared by air
  traffic control.
- **Convoy route** — the route published each morning for vehicles that must
  cross a surface being treated in winter, escorted by the works team.
- **Duty controller** — the airside operations officer on duty in the control
  room, who grades occurrences and directs vehicle movement.
- **Escort ratio** — the number of visitors one escort may control at a time,
  set in clause 4.4.
- **Fire lane** — the route kept clear at all times for emergency vehicles,
  marked in red and hatched in white.
- **FOD bin** — the container placed at each stand row for foreign object
  debris collected by badge holders.
- **Gate line** — the painted line at an access gate that a vehicle does not
  cross until the gate is fully open.
- **Holding line** — the painted line at which a vehicle or an aircraft stops
  short of a runway or a taxiway.
- **Hydrant pit** — the recessed pit that houses a fuel hydrant, marked in
  yellow.
- **Jet blast** — the air movement produced by an aircraft engine that has a
  hazard to people and vehicles behind the aircraft.
- **Landside service road** — the road inside the security fence that links
  the access gates to the depots and the terminal forecourts, and that serves
  no aircraft.
- **Lead-in line** — the painted line that guides an aircraft from a taxiway
  onto a stand.
- **Marshalling area** — the marked area on the apron where vehicles wait
  until they are called to an aircraft.
- **Movement surface** — any surface on which an aircraft, a vehicle or a
  person may move, including the runway, the taxiways, the aprons and the
  service roads.
- **Manoeuvring area** — the runway and the taxiways, excluding the aprons,
  where aircraft movement is controlled by air traffic control.
- **Obstacle limitation surface** — the volume of airspace that must be kept
  clear of obstacles around the runway and the approach paths.
- **Occurrence** — an event defined in clause 12.2, reported under clause 12.
- **Pass office** — the unit that issues airside badges and records the
  training and assessment of badge holders.
- **Permit holder** — the badge holder named on a vehicle permit, accountable
  for the vehicle's compliance with clause 6.
- **Plant tag** — the tag fixed to an item of plant that records its last
  inspection and the date of the next one.
- **Precision approach path** — the published descent path for an aircraft on
  final approach, protected by the obstacle limitation surfaces.
- **Rapid exit taxiway** — a taxiway laid at an angle to the runway to allow
  an aircraft to leave at speed.
- **Runway strip** — the area around the runway that must be kept clear of
  vehicles and equipment unless a clearance has been given.
- **Safety action** — a finding or an instruction recorded in the safety
  actions register against an owner and a date.
- **Stand entry guidance** — the visual system that shows a pilot the position
  of the aircraft on the stand.
- **Stand holding line** — the painted line at the entrance to a stand area
  at which a vehicle waits.
- **Stand safety area** — the area around a stand in which an aircraft may
  move and in which a vehicle may not be parked.
- **Taxilane** — the part of the apron used by aircraft to move between the
  stand rows and the taxiway system.
- **Vehicle marshalling area** — see marshalling area.
- **Vehicle permit register** — the record kept under clause 6.2 of every
  permit issued, renewed, lapsed and withdrawn.
- **Waiver register** — the record kept under clause 3.3 of every waiver
  granted, with its reason and its end date.
- **Wildlife log** — the record kept by the wildlife unit of sightings,
  dispersals and strikes.

## Appendix B — Permit classes and endorsements

### B.1 Permit classes

Every vehicle permit falls into one of the classes below. The class is printed
on the permit and decides the routes the vehicle may use and the gates it may
pass through.

| Class | Vehicle type | Routes | Gates |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Airside operations and security patrol | All movement surfaces | G1, G2, G4 |
| P2 | Aircraft handling plant and tugs | Aprons and taxilanes | G1, G2 |
| P3 | Fuel bowsers | Aprons, hydrant routes | G1, G2 |
| P4 | Cargo vehicles | Cargo apron and cargo road | G2 |
| P5 | Catering and cleaning | Aprons and service roads | G1, G7 |
| P6 | Maintenance base vehicles | Base roads and service roads | G4, G7 |
| P7 | Service-road-only vehicles | Landside service roads | G7, G11 |

### B.2 Class P7

Class P7 covers vehicles that work entirely on the landside service roads:
depot shunt vehicles, stores vans, the shuttle bus fleet based at the
Northgate depot and the groundworks trucks that serve the landside buildings.
A P7 vehicle holds no apron entitlement and its permit carries the marking
"service roads" in place of an apron route. A P7 vehicle that is required at
an aircraft is re-permitted in another class before it enters the apron, and
the re-permitting is recorded in the vehicle permit register.

### B.3 Endorsement combinations

A driver holds the endorsements their duties need. The combinations below are
the ones airside operations issues most often, and each combination is
assessed and refreshed as clause 13.4 sets.

| Combination | Held by |
|---|---|
| D | Stores and cleaning drivers |
| D, E | Supervisors and team leaders |
| D, R | Patrol drivers and control room staff |
| D, H | Works team plant operators |
| D, R, H | Airside operations duty officers |
| D, M, R | Marshalling team |

### B.4 Permit checks at the gate

A gate officer checks the permit's class against the route the driver intends
to use. A driver whose permit does not carry the apron entitlement is directed
to the service road and the attempt is recorded. A second attempt by the same
vehicle in the same week is reported to airside operations, which reviews the
permit and the driver's badge endorsements.

## Appendix C — Site plan notes

### C.1 Surfaces by area

The table below lists the areas of the airport, the surface type and the
signal or marking that identifies it. The table is read with the site plan
issued to every badge holder at induction.

| Area | Surface | Identifying marking |
|---|---|---|
| Runway 09/27 | Asphalt, grooved | White threshold bars, runway designator |
| Parallel taxiway T1 | Asphalt | Yellow centreline, blue edge lights |
| Rapid exit taxiways | Asphalt | Yellow centreline, green exit lights |
| Terminal apron, stand rows A to D | Concrete | Yellow stand lead-in lines, red stand numbers |
| Cargo apron | Concrete | White parking boxes, blue edge line |
| General aviation apron | Concrete | White parking boxes |
| Maintenance base apron | Asphalt | Yellow lines, base unit code |
| Landside service road | Asphalt | White edge lines, no aircraft marking |
| Depot yards | Concrete | White bays, green pedestrian walkways |
| Terminal forecourts | Block paving | Yellow box junction, white walkways |

### C.2 Stand rows and capacities

| Row | Stands | Aircraft class | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 1 to 9 | Narrow body | Walkway along the front of the row |
| B | 10 to 16 | Narrow body | Shared with the cargo road at stand 16 |
| C | 17 to 24 | Narrow body and regional | Remote stands, no air bridge |
| D | 25 to 30 | Wide body | Two air bridges at stands 27 and 29 |
| Cargo | C1 to C8 | Freighter | Ground handling by the cargo agent |
| General aviation | GA1 to GA6 | Light aircraft | Self-manoeuvring stands |

### C.3 Fixed equipment

Fixed equipment on the apron comprises fuel hydrants at every second stand,
potable water points at the head of each stand, ground power units at stands
1 to 16, and stand entry guidance at stands 17 to 30. A badge holder reports
damage to any fixed equipment to airside operations control, which passes the
report to the unit that owns the equipment.

### C.4 Walkways and crossing points

Painted walkways run along the front of each stand row and along the service
road. A pedestrian crosses a vehicle route only at a marked crossing point
and only after making eye contact with the driver of any vehicle in the
vicinity. A pedestrian does not use a radio, a telephone or earphones while
crossing a vehicle route.

## Appendix D — Site-specific variations

This appendix records the variations to the body of this handbook that apply
at particular sites of Meridian Airport. Each variation names the site, the
clause it varies and the value that applies there. A variation applies only
to the site and the class of vehicle or person it names; everywhere else the
body of the handbook stands unchanged. The variations are agreed with the
safety and compliance board and are reviewed with the handbook.

### D.1 Northgate depot

The Northgate depot stands at the east end of the landside service road and
is reached through gate G11. Vehicles based at the depot work only on the
landside service roads: the depot shunt vehicles, the stores vans and the
shuttle bus fleet that runs between the depot and the terminal forecourts.
They are permitted in class P7 and hold no apron entitlement.

**D.1.1 Permit validity for depot-based service-road vehicles.** A class P7
vehicle based at the Northgate depot and used only on the landside service
roads holds a permit valid for 36 months, in place of the validity given in
clause 6.1.1. The depot manager confirms in writing that the vehicle does not
enter the apron, and the confirmation is filed with the application. A P7
vehicle that begins to work on the apron is re-permitted in class P5 or P6,
takes the validity in clause 6.1.1, and is presented for the vehicle standards
check in clause 6.3 before its first apron movement.

**D.1.2 Gate hours.** Gate G11 is staffed between 05:30 and 21:00. Outside
those hours a depot vehicle enters by gate G7 and reports to airside
operations control on arrival.

### D.2 Maintenance base apron

Vehicles of the maintenance base that stay within the base apron and the base
roads are exempt from the beacon requirement in clause 7.4 while they are
inside the base boundary, and use dipped headlights instead. A base vehicle
that leaves the base boundary displays a flashing amber beacon as clause 7.4
requires.

### D.3 Cargo apron

The cargo apron operates a one-way route for vehicles between 22:00 and 06:00
during the freighter programme. The route is published weekly by airside
operations and is marked with temporary signage; a driver who cannot follow
the route reports to control and waits for an escort.

### D.4 General aviation apron

Light aircraft on the general aviation apron are self-manoeuvring, so vehicles
give way to an aircraft that is taxiing on the apron as well as to one that is
on the manoeuvring area. Clause 7.2 is read accordingly at this apron.

## Appendix E — Revision history

| Revision | Issued | Summary |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | 14 October 2025 | Handbook re-issued as a single document; clause numbering fixed |
| 8 | 9 December 2025 | Winter operations plan and snow clearance priorities added |
| 9 | 24 February 2026 | Access gate table and visitor escort ratio revised |
| 10 | 16 March 2026 | Occurrence categories revised; safety actions register introduced |
| 11 | 6 April 2026 | Vehicle permit classes and endorsements consolidated in appendix B; site variations consolidated in appendix D |

A clause that is withdrawn keeps its number, and the withdrawal is recorded
below the revision that made it. Clause 5.4.2 was withdrawn at revision 10
and its number is retired. Clause 9.7 was withdrawn at revision 9 and its
number is retired.

The next review falls in September 2026. Comments on this revision are sent to
airside operations, which answers them in writing and carries accepted changes
into the next revision.
